meantobvs

Missing data and other extensions to Bayesian Variable Selection


Overview

meantobvs is an R package that implements Bayesian Variable Selection based on Bayes factors.

The software is meant to be the variable selection solution for a broad range of problems. It applies to both linear and generalized linear models, through an intuitive interface, similar to the well-known lm and glm functions. The flexible implementation allows the advanced user to customize priors from a set of popular choices (Bayarri et al, 2012; Li and Clyde, 2018). Fast approximations such as the BIC (Schwarz, 1978) and TBF (Held, Sabanés and Gravestock, 2015) are also available. Default choices are fully automatic and meant for objective Bayesian variable selection, while accounting for multiplicity issues (Scott and Berger, 2008). The process can be done through exact algorithms, to perform fast computations in problems of small to moderate size, and heuristic sampling methods to solve large complex problems.

meantobvs deals with several issues that standard variable selection methods cannot, such as missing data and categorical variables.


Methodology

BVS

When missingness occurs, standard variable selection methods cannot be applied, while multiple imputation procedures depend on the variables included, leading to a catch-22 situation. As other statistical areas, variable selection is not free from the bias consequence of the missing mechanism. In order to account for both sources of uncertainty, García-Donato et al. (2025) integrate missing data into the marginal likelihood. meantobvs implements this methodology in linear and generalized linear models via an average over the marginal of several imputed datasets. Thereby the derived model posterior becomes a weighted mean to the Bayesian variable selection method.



The posterior distribution over the model space is given through Bayes’ theorem: \[ P(M_i | {\tt{data}}) = P(M_i)\ AvB_i({\tt{data}})\ /\ C, \] where \(AvB_i\) is the Average Bayes factor of \(M_i\) to \(M_0\) (null model) under missing data, \(P(M_i)\) is the prior probability of \(M_i\) and \(C\) is the normalizing constant. \(AvB_i\) is defined as the average of the corresponding data-driven standard BFs: \[ AvB_i = [\ B_i({\tt{complete\ data}}_1)\ +\ ...\ +\ B_i({\tt{complete\ data}}_{\tt {n.imp}})\ ]\ /\ {\tt {n.imp}}, \] where \(B_i({\tt{complete\ data}}_j)\) corresponds to the BF for model \(M_i\) to \(M_0\) under the \(j\)-th imputed dataset. Data-driven BF can be either computed using popular g-prior choices or approximated with the BIC (Schwarz, 1978) or the test-based BF (Held, Gravestock and Sabanés, 2015).

In the presence of categorical variables (factors), the uncertainty regarding the levels definition and its nature has not received so much attention. A naive approach makes results highly dependent on the specification, usually somehow arbitrary, and changes probabilities drastically, due to multiplicity issues (Scott and Berger, 2010). meantobvs by default assess factors themselves by averaging over the set of models with at least one active dummy variable (García-Donato and Paulo, 2022):



\[ P(M_i | {\tt{data}}) = P(M_i)\ B_i({\tt{data}})\ /\ C, \] where \(B_i({\tt{data}}) = \sum_k P(M_{ik})\ B_k({\tt{data}})\) corresponds to the BF for model \(M_i\) to \(M_0\) if \(M_i\) has an active factor and \(M_{ik}\) are the submodel space made by the different possible active levels of the factor. The methodology computes a posterior over the model space made up by the factors, properly accounting for the reference level.

The posterior distribution can be summarized with its mode (the highest posterior probability model) and marginal posterior inclusion probabilities for each competing variable (a measure of relative importance) along with the median probability model (Barbieri and Berger, 2004), to answer the user questions.


Installing steps

To install the latest development version, you can use install_github from the devtools package:

## install devtools if necessary
install.packages('devtools')
library(devtools)
## get the package from github
install_github('camulro/meantobvs', dependencies = TRUE)


Usage

Perform variable selection on linear regression models as follows.

  • Exhaustive enumeration of the model space defined by inclusion/exclusion of the different variables specified by the full model.
# Keep the eight models generated by three candidate covariates,
# BIC approximation for BF by default, few imputations for simplicity, real analyses need more.
f <- gr56092 ~ 1 + lifee060 + gdpsh60l + p60
dataS97.meantobvs <- bvs.lm(
   formula = f, data = dataS97, n.keep = 8, n.imp = 2, imp.seed = 1
)
NA values found on the response variable. We are going to omit these observations.

Code: HPM stands for Highest posterior Probability Model and
      MPM for Median Probability Model.


  • Huge model spaces: approximation of the posterior model distribution through a Gibbs sampling algorithm.
#Short chain for the example; real analyses need more iterations.
#Few imputations for simplicity, real analyses need more.
dataS97.meantobvs <- gibbsbvs.lm(
 formula = gr56092 ~ .,
 data = dataS97, n.iter = 200, n.burnin = 50, n.imp = 2,
 Gibbs.seed = 1, imp.seed = 1
)

#A plot with the posterior inclusion probabilities for each competing variable
#and the dimension probability of the true model:
plot(dataS97.meantobvs)



  • User given model space.
#Define the list of competing models
models.list <- list(
   M0 = gr56092 ~ 1,
   M1 = gr56092 ~ lifee060,
   M2 = gr56092 ~ gdpsh60l,
   M3 = gr56092 ~ p60,
   M7 = gr56092 ~ lifee060 + gdpsh60l + p60
 )

#Few imputations for simplicity, real analyses need more.
dataS97.meantobtest <- btest.lm(
   data = dataS97, models = models.list, n.imp = 2, imp.seed = 1
)

#Show the results:
dataS97.meantobtest

Perform variable selection on generalized linear models as follows.

  • Exhaustive enumeration of the model space defined by inclusion/exclusion of the different variables specified by the full model.
#Indian Prime Diabetes Data
diabetes.meantobvs <- bvs.glm(
 formula = f, data = diabetes, family = binomial(), n.keep = 32,
 n.imp = 10, imp.seed = 1
)

#Show the results:
diabetes.meantobvs

#Summ up the results:
summary(diabetes.meantobvs)


  • Huge model spaces: approximation of the posterior model distribution through a Gibbs sampling algorithm.
#Default choices are: BIC approximation and ScottBerger prior.
#Use a short chain for the example; real analyses need more iterations.
#Few imputations for simplicity, real analyses need more.
diabetes.meantobvs <- gibbsbvs.glm(
 formula = Outcome ~  ., data = diabetes, family = binomial(),
 n.iter = 200, n.burnin = 50, n.imp = 2, Gibbs.seed = 1, imp.seed = 1
)

#Summ up the results:
summary(diabetes.meantobvs)


  • User given model space.
#Define the list of competing models
models.list = list(
   M0 = Outcome ~ 1,
   M1 = Outcome ~ Pregnancies,
   M2 = Outcome ~ Glucose,
   M3 = Outcome ~ Insulin,
   M4 = Outcome ~ Pregnancies + Glucose,
   M5 = Outcome ~ Pregnancies + Insulin,
   M6 = Outcome ~ Pregnancies + Glucose + Insulin
)

#Default choices are: BIC approximation and Constant prior.
#Few imputations for simplicity, real analyses need more.
diabetes.meantobtest <- mbtest.glm(
   data = diabetes, models = models.list, family = binomial(),
   n.imp = 2, imp.seed = 1
)


#Show the results:
diabetes.meantobtest
